Produces well-marbled meat with superior flavor — the preferred breed for premium pork in Japan (Kurobuta). Moderate fat coverage. Berkshire pork commands a premium for its taste and texture. Mature weight 200-250 kg. Good mothers with 8-10 piglets per litter. Hardy and adaptable to outdoor systems. - **Gloucestershire Old Spot**: White with black spots, large droo...

Black with white points (feet, face, tail). Compact, early-maturing. Produces well-marbled meat with superior flavor — the preferred breed for premium pork in Japan (Kurobuta). Moderate fat coverage. Berkshire pork commands a premium for its taste and texture. Mature weight 200-250 kg. Good mothers with 8-10 piglets per litter. Hardy and adaptable to outdoor systems.

White with black spots, large drooping ears. A traditional orchard pig — developed to clean up fallen fruit in cider orchards. Excellent foragers on pasture. Docile temperament. Produces high-quality pork and good lard yields. Hardy in cold, wet conditions.

(selected for length and lean meat): - **Tamworth**: Ginger-red, long-bodied, erect ears. The most "primitive" looking of British breeds — long snout, lean build. Exceptional foraging ability — one of the best breeds for woodland and pasture systems. Produces long sides ideal for bacon curing. Hardier and more disease-resistant than most modern breeds. Litter size 6-10. Slower growing than commercial hybrids (market weight at 8-10 months) but thriving on low-quality feed. - **Large White (Yor...

Ginger-red, long-bodied, erect ears. The most "primitive" looking of British breeds — long snout, lean build. Exceptional foraging ability — one of the best breeds for woodland and pasture systems. Produces long sides ideal for bacon curing. Hardier and more disease-resistant than most modern breeds. Litter size 6-10. Slower growing than commercial hybrids (market weight at 8-10 months) but thriving on low-quality feed.

All white, erect ears, long body. The most numerous pig breed worldwide. Large litters (10-14 piglets). Fast growth. The foundation of commercial hybrid pig production — Large White × Landrace crosses dominate industrial systems. Good mothers. Less hardy for outdoor systems than traditional breeds.
White, lop-eared, long-bodied. Excellent maternal breed with large litters and good milking ability. Used primarily as a dam line in crossbreeding programs. Docile and easy to manage.

Red-brown, drooping ears, muscular. Used as a terminal sire in crossbreeding — Duroc genetics add growth rate, feed efficiency, and meat quality (especially marbling) to commercial crossbred pigs. Hardy and adaptable. Faster-growing than traditional breeds.

(traditional woodland grazing): Pannage is the practice of releasing domestic pigs into oak and beech forests in autumn to feed on fallen acorns and beechnuts (mast). This tradition dates to antiquity and persists in parts of Europe (notably the New Forest in England and the dehesa system in Spain for Iberian ham production).

Vegetable peelings, fruit waste, plate scrapings, stale bread. Avoid meat scraps from other pigs (disease transmission risk, especially African swine fever and classical swine fever) and excessive salt.

The liquid byproduct of cheese making. Feeding whey to pigs is one of the oldest integrated farming practices — dairy and pig production are naturally complementary. Whey contains protein (0.6-0.8%), lactose (4-5%), and minerals. Pigs on whey require less grain supplement.

Cull fruits and vegetables from gardens and orchards, crop harvest byproducts (pea vines, bean pods, corn stalks chopped, sugar beet pulp). Not all crop residues are suitable — some are too fibrous or low in digestible nutrients without processing.
Moderate protein (18-26% on a dry matter basis), high fiber. Useful supplementary feed, especially for gestating sows.
90-110 kg live weight at 5-7 months. Carcass yield 75-80%. Standard commodity pork.
70-80 kg at 8-10 months (slower growth, but developing more complex flavor and firmer fat). Carcass yield 70-75%. Superior eating quality.

140-170 kg at 12-18 months. Used for Parma ham, Iberian ham, and other dry-cured products where larger muscles and more fat are desirable. The extended growth period develops intramuscular fat and complex flavor.

Render by cutting fat into small pieces, heating slowly at 100-120°C until fat liquifies and cracklings (crispy residue) float. Strain through cloth. Yield: 70-85% of fat weight. Liver, kidneys, heart, intestines (sausage casings — clean thoroughly, scrape mucosa, salt and store), blood (blood sausage, black pudding) - **Bristles**: Boar bristles from the neck and back are used for hairbrushes, paint brushes, and shaving brushes. Harvest at slaughter, clean, and sort by length and stiffness. - **Pigskin**: Tans into a durable, flexible leather used for garments, gloves, and footballs. Boars are large, powerful, and potentially dangerous animals. A mature boar weighs 200-350 kg with tusks that can inflict severe lacerations. Critical safety rules: - **Never turn your back on a boar.** Always face the boar and maintain awareness of his position. - Use a boar board (a solid wooden or metal shield, approximately 1 m × 1.2 m) as a physical barrier between you and the boar during handling. - Boars signal aggression by chomping (clicking their jaws), frothing at the mouth, and si...

Mix pig manure with carbon-rich bedding (straw, sawdust) at a C:N ratio of 25-30:1. Composting at 55-65°C for 3-4 weeks kills pathogens (Salmonella, E. coli) and reduces odor. Finished compost is a high-value soil amendment.

Pig manure can be applied to cropland, but fresh manure should be incorporated into soil immediately to prevent nitrogen loss (ammonia volatilization) and runoff. Apply at rates that match crop nutrient needs — excess application causes nitrogen leaching into groundwater.
(*Brachyspira hyodysenteriae*): Severe bloody diarrhea, high morbidity. Transmitted by fecal-oral route. Treat with antimicrobials; prevent with hygiene and all-in/all-out management.

Viral disease causing reproductive failure (abortions, stillbirths, weak piglets) and respiratory disease in growing pigs. Highly contagious. No treatment — management focuses on biosecurity, herd immunity, and vaccination where available.

Devastating viral disease with near-100% mortality in domestic pigs. No vaccine, no treatment. Transmitted by direct contact, contaminated equipment, and soft ticks. Strict biosecurity (quarantine, no pork product importation, no contact with wild boar) is the only prevention. ASF has caused massive losses in global pig populations.

(*Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae*): Diamond-shaped skin lesions, fever, arthritis. Survives in soil. Treat with penicillin. Vaccinate sows and boars annually. Can transmit to humans (erysipeloid — painful skin infection from handling infected animals or carcasses).
Causes reproductive failure in gilts (mummified fetuses, stillbirths). Widespread in pig populations. Vaccinate gilts before first breeding.

Pigs carry several diseases transmissible to humans. Erysipeloid (skin infection from handling infected animals), trichinellosis (from eating undercooked pork — Trichinella spiralis larvae encyst in muscle tissue; prevented by cooking pork to 71°C or freezing at -15°C for 20+ days), Salmonella, and influenza (pigs are mixing vessels for avian, swine, and human influenza viruses — they can generate novel pandemic strains). Always cook pork thoroughly. Wear gloves when handling pig manure.
See Boar Management section above. A boar is the most dangerous farm animal relative to its size. Treat with constant respect.

Sows are large and clumsy with piglets. The guard rails and heated creep area described in Farrowing Management are essential — without them, 20-30% of piglets may be crushed in the first 3 days. Monitor closely during the first 48 hours post-farrowing.

Pigs have poor eyesight but excellent hearing and a strong sense of smell. Move pigs calmly using boards (solid barriers) and gentle persuasion — never use electric prods or excessive force, which causes panic and injuries. Pigs move toward light and away from loud noises. A sorting board (a large, solid panel) allows safe redirection without physical contact.

Pigs kept in dirty conditions are more susceptible to disease and parasites. Maintain clean water, fresh bedding, and adequate drainage. The stereotype of pigs as "dirty" animals is a product of poor management — given the choice, pigs eliminate in one area of their pen and keep their sleeping area clean.

Modern commercial pigs reach 100 kg live weight at 140-160 days (20-23 weeks) with a feed conversion ratio of 2.5-2.8 kg feed per kg gain. Heritage breeds on pasture reach 80-100 kg at 200-280 days (29-40 weeks) with FCR of 3.5-4.5. A single sow producing 2.0-2.2 litters per year (18-24 piglets weaned annually) generates 1,620-2,400 kg of live weight per year — approximately 1,200-1,800 kg of carcass weight. At $2.00-3.50 per kg carcass weight, each sow generates $2,400-6,300 in annual gross ...

Pigs achieve 80-85% utilization of live weight — the highest of any livestock species. A 100 kg pig yields a 75-80 kg dressed carcass that breaks down into 55-60 kg of retail cuts, 12-15 kg of renderable fat, 5-7 kg of bone, and 3-5 kg of offal (liver, heart, kidneys, intestines). Lard yield from fat-type breeds: 20-30 kg per animal. Bristle yield: 100-200 g per animal (neck and back region). Intestines from one pig provide 15-20 m of sausage casing (after cleaning, scraping, and salting).

Protozoan parasite (*Eimeria* spp.) causing bloody diarrhea and weight loss in young birds. Prevent with clean dry litter and coccidiostat in feed (or allow controlled exposure to build immunity). Treat with amprolium in water.

Herpesvirus causing tumors and paralysis. Vaccinate chicks at day 1 (subcutaneous injection of live attenuated vaccine). Nearly 100% effective when properly administered. Without vaccination, mortality can reach 30-60% in infected flocks.
Viral infection causing respiratory distress, neurological symptoms, and sudden death. Highly contagious. No treatment — prevention through biosecurity and vaccination where the disease is endemic.

Viral disease with strains ranging from low-pathogenic (mild respiratory symptoms) to highly pathogenic (rapid mortality up to 90-100%). Biosecurity: prevent contact with wild waterfowl (primary reservoir), quarantine new birds for 30 days, disinfect equipment between flocks.
Viral disease causing scabby lesions on comb, wattles, and skin. Transmitted by mosquitoes. Usually self-limiting with low mortality. Vaccine available.
Causes anemia, reduced egg production. Treat with permethrin dust or diatomaceous earth in dust baths.
Flat, straw-colored insects on skin and feathers. Cause irritation and reduced production. Treat with dust baths containing wood ash and diatomaceous earth.

(roundworms, capillary worms, tapeworms): Cause weight loss and reduced egg production. Prevent by rotating pasture, keeping litter dry. Treat with fenbendazole or ivermectin (observe egg withdrawal period).

Same protozoan parasite as in chickens. Prevent with clean, dry conditions and proper stocking density. Wire-bottom cages reduce exposure compared to floor systems.

Eggs stuck in the oviduct, particularly in first-time layers and overweight hens. Provide adequate calcium and ensure proper calcium-to-phosphorus ratio in feed.

Ducks foraging in stagnant water or decaying vegetation are susceptible to *Clostridium botulinum* type C toxin (not the human type A). Causes progressive paralysis ("limberneck"). Prevent by keeping water clean and removing decaying organic matter from duck areas. Treat with type C antitoxin if available.

Ducks on the ground are vulnerable at night. Secure them in a predator-proof shelter from dusk to dawn.

Practiced in some regions but controversial. Geese can be plucked of mature down 2-3 times per year during natural molting periods, yielding 60-100 g per plucking. Geese must be handled carefully to avoid skin tears. Some regions prohibit live-plucking.
Collect naturally shed down and feathers from goose shelters during molting season (summer). Labor-intensive and yields are low, but it is non-invasive.

Fill for quilts, sleeping bags, jackets, and pillows. Down provides approximately 3-4 times the insulation per unit weight of synthetic alternatives. Measured in fill power (volume in cubic inches that 1 ounce of down occupies): good quality 500-600, premium 700-800, exceptional 800+. Fill power degrades with moisture and compression — store down items uncompressed in dry conditions.
A standard pillow requires 500-800 g of down. A queen-size duvet requires 800-1200 g depending on warmth rating.

Geese cannot physically deter large predators (coyotes, wolves, large birds of prey). They are effective as alarm systems and small-predator deterrents. Pair guardian geese with secure nighttime housing for the rest of the flock.
Same as ducks — twisted wing joint from excess protein/calories during rapid growth. Reduce protein to 14-15% after 4 weeks if symptoms appear.
Risk from stagnant water. Keep water sources clean and flowing where possible.
Heavy geese on rough or abrasive surfaces develop foot pad infections. Provide clean, smooth flooring and pasture.
Acquired from eating earthworms. Causes gasping and neck stretching. Treat with fenbendazole.

Goslings are vulnerable to all small predators. Adult geese are large enough to deter most raptors and small mammals, but foxes, coyotes, and loose dogs will kill adult geese. Secure housing at night is essential.

The average goose carcass contains 800-1200 g of subcutaneous fat, considerably more than duck — a single Embden goose yields 500-1000 g of rendered fat with a smoke point of approximately 190°C.

A mature goose yields 100-150 g of raw down (60-100 g after cleaning and sorting). Premium goose down achieves fill power of 500-600 for standard quality, 600-700 for good, and 700-800+ for exceptional quality.

The primary flight feathers of geese were the standard writing instrument for over 1,000 years before steel nibs became common in the 1830s. A single goose provides 5-10 suitable quill feathers per year from its outermost primaries.
Record laying start date, total eggs per goose per season, and average clutch size. Target: 30-50 eggs per goose per year for production breeds, 50-80 for Chinese geese.
Record hatch rate (target 60-75% from fertile eggs), gosling mortality by week, and causes of loss. First-week mortality should not exceed 5% with proper brooding at 30-32°C.

Estimate forage consumption as a percentage of total diet by tracking supplemental grain fed versus expected full-ration consumption. On good pasture, geese should require only 50-100 g supplemental grain per day.

Track gander-to-goose ratio (optimal 1:2-3), fertility rate (percentage of eggs showing development when candled at day 7), and hatch rate per breeding pair. Replace ganders producing less than 50% fertility.

Record weight of raw down per bird at processing. Target: 100-150 g per mature goose. Track processed down quality (fill power, measured as cubic inches per ounce) to optimize harvest timing and processing methods.

The most common variety. Dark grey plumage densely spotted with white pearled dots. Excellent foragers, good egg production. Standard size: 1.3-1.6 kg. Wild-type coloration provides excellent camouflage from aerial predators on range.

Light silver-grey plumage with white pearling. Same size and productivity as Pearl Grey. Preferred by some keepers for calmer temperament and distinctive appearance. Feather coloration is a single-gene dilute of the pearl grey.
All-white plumage. Less camouflage protection on range but clean carcass appearance after processing. Slightly less hardy than pigmented varieties.
Iridescent purple-grey plumage. Less common but same utility as Pearl Grey.

A distinct species (*Acryllium vulturine*) rather than a variety. Striking blue and white plumage with long hackle feathers. More ornamental, less cold-hardy. Rarely raised for meat outside tropical climates.

(0-6 weeks): Keets (guinea fowl chicks) are tiny and extremely fragile during the first 2 weeks — mortality can reach 30-50% without careful management. Critical requirements: - **Temperature**: Start at 35-38°C in the brooder, reduce by 3°C per week. Keets chill easily and will pile in corners, smothering each other. - **Draft prevention**: Even a slight draft at floor level can kill keets. Use solid brooder guards (30-40 cm high) in a circle to prevent corner-piling. - **Feed**: High-protei...
Start at 35-38°C in the brooder, reduce by 3°C per week. Keets chill easily and will pile in corners, smothering each other.
Even a slight draft at floor level can kill keets. Use solid brooder guards (30-40 cm high) in a circle to prevent corner-piling.
High-protein starter (24-28% protein) — higher than chicken starter. Crumbles or mash. Spread feed on paper towels or shallow trays for the first 3-5 days so keets can find it easily.
Paper towels or burlap for the first 3-5 days (keets eat wood shavings and can develop fatal impaction). Switch to wood shavings after day 5.
The first 2 weeks are critical. Proper temperature, draft prevention, and appropriate feed reduce losses dramatically.
Tiny keets on range are extremely vulnerable. Confine until 6-8 weeks before allowing range access.
In very cold climates (-15°C and below), guinea fowl wattles can suffer frostbite. Provide draft-free shelter.
Keets may eat inappropriate bedding material (wood shavings, straw), causing fatal intestinal blockage. Use paper towels for first 5 days.

Guinea fowl originate from sub-Saharan Africa and thrive in hot, dry conditions (30-40°C daytime temperatures). They tolerate heat significantly better than chickens and continue foraging actively when chickens seek shade.

In northern latitudes (above 40 degrees north), guinea fowl are seasonal layers from March through September, governed by the 14+ hour daylight threshold. Egg production ceases when daylight drops below 12 hours.
Guinea fowl excel in dry environments where chickens struggle with heat stress and respiratory disease. They require only 100-200 mL water per day versus 250-500 mL for chickens of comparable size.
Guinea fowl reach market weight of 1.0-1.5 kg dressed at 12-16 weeks. Process identically to chickens: dispatch, bleed 60-90 seconds, scald at 55-60°C for 30-45 seconds, pluck, eviscerate.

Guinea eggs weigh 35-40 g with extremely hard, thick shells (0.3-0.4 mm versus 0.2-0.3 mm for chicken eggs), providing natural protection and extending shelf life to 3-4 weeks at room temperature versus 2 weeks for chicken eggs.
Guinea fowl feathers are valued for fly-tying, hat-making, and ornamental crafts. The distinctive spotted pearl-grey plumage commands prices 2-3 times higher than chicken feathers in craft markets.

Guinea fowl manure (approximately 1.5% N, 1.0% P, 0.5% K fresh weight) is comparable to chicken manure in nutrient density, composting to a stable fertilizer over 6-8 weeks when mixed with carbon-rich bedding material.

Maintain a running count of birds by age group and sex. Guinea fowl are long-lived (10-15 years) but egg production declines after year 5-6, dropping to 40-60% of peak output and warranting culling for meat.

Track fertility rate (candle eggs at 7-10 days — fertile eggs show a visible spider-web blood vessel network), hatch rate from fertile eggs (target 60-75%), and keet survival to 8 weeks (target above 70%).

Record all predator kills with date, suspected predator species, and location. Free-range guinea fowl experience 5-15% annual losses to hawks, owls, foxes, and coyotes depending on local predator density.
Monitor tick and insect populations quarterly using drag-sampling — drag a 1 m² white cloth through range vegetation for 50 m and count attached ticks per sample.
Record all input costs (feed, supplements, medication, equipment) against production output (eggs, meat, live birds sold) to calculate cost per unit of protein produced.

Replace 20-25% of breeding hens annually to maintain flock productivity. Select replacement hens from the earliest-hatched keets each season — early hatching correlates with vigor and longevity in guinea fowl.

(meat-focused): - **King**: The primary squab breed worldwide. Large-bodied, 600-800 g live weight. Squab reach 450-550 g at 26-28 days. White, silver, red, and yellow varieties. Reliable breeders, producing 10-14 squab pairs per year. Good temperament, adapt well to loft confinement. - **Carneau**: French squab breed. 550-700 g live weight. Squab reach 400-500 g at 26-30 days. Good foragers if allowed to range. Red, yellow, and white varieties. Hardy and disease-resistant. Slightly less prol...

The primary squab breed worldwide. Large-bodied, 600-800 g live weight. Squab reach 450-550 g at 26-28 days. White, silver, red, and yellow varieties. Reliable breeders, producing 10-14 squab pairs per year. Good temperament, adapt well to loft confinement.

French squab breed. 550-700 g live weight. Squab reach 400-500 g at 26-30 days. Good foragers if allowed to range. Red, yellow, and white varieties. Hardy and disease-resistant. Slightly less prolific than Kings but excellent meat quality.
Large French breed developed for maximum squab size. 700-900 g live weight. Squab can reach 500-600 g dressed. Lower reproduction rate (8-10 squab pairs per year) but premium weight per bird.
Auto-sexing breed (males and females have different feather colors as nestlings, enabling early sorting). Good squab production and rapid growth. 600-750 g live weight.

Medium-sized (350-450 g), bred for navigation and endurance. Can carry messages over 1000+ km. Squab production is moderate (6-8 pairs per year) but the breed's homing ability is irreplaceable for communication.
Large utility breed, good for squab and as a foster parent for other breeds. Calm temperament.

(for homing pigeons): One-way trap doors (bobs) allow pigeons to enter but not exit through the trap hole. This is essential for racing and messaging pigeons — they can return home but cannot leave without the keeper opening an exit. Simple construction: a row of thin metal or wooden rods hung vertically in the entry hole, spaced 4-5 cm apart. Pigeons push through inward but cannot push them outward to escape.
Neurological disease causing twisting of the neck, incoordination, and death. Preventable by vaccination. Highly contagious — vaccinate all birds annually.
Protozoan infection of the throat and crop, common in squab. Yellow cheesy growths in the mouth interfere with feeding. Treat with metronidazole. Prevent by keeping water sources clean.
Intestinal protozoan parasite. More common in damp lofts. Symptoms: weight loss, diarrhea. Treat with amprolium. Prevent with dry, clean loft conditions.
Mycoplasma and chlamydia (ornithosis) cause respiratory distress. Good ventilation is preventive. Treatable with tetracycline-class antibiotics.
Pigeon lice, mites, and pigeon flies. Regular dusting with diatomaceous earth or pyrethrin-based powder. Keep nest boxes clean.

Pigeon guano must be aged or composted before use — fresh guano at 4-5% nitrogen will burn plant roots on contact. Compost with 3 parts carbon-rich material (straw, leaves, sawdust) to 1 part guano by volume for 8-12 weeks.

Pigeon feathers are soft and downy, suitable for pillow stuffing and insulation. A single pigeon yields 15-25 g of mixed feathers. Pigeon primary flight feathers were historically used as quill pens for fine writing before being superseded by goose quills.
Record squab produced per pair per year. Target: 10-14 squab pairs per year for King pigeons, 8-10 for Mondains. A pair producing fewer than 6 squab in 6 months should be evaluated for replacement.

Weigh a sample of 10-15 squab at harvest each month. Target dressed weight: 400-550 g for Kings, 350-450 g for Carneaux. A declining trend of more than 10% over 2 months indicates nutritional or health problems.

Track guano collection volume weekly. A flock of 50 breeding pairs should produce approximately 500-750 kg of guano per year (10-15 kg per pair). Declining guano production often indicates inadequate nutrition before it shows in squab production.

Track total grain consumption per week against squab output. Target: approximately 3-4 kg of adult feed produces 1 kg of squab live weight. Feed costs should represent 60-70% of total production costs.

Record all mortality with date, age, and symptoms. Target annual mortality: under 10% for adult breeders. Investigate any month with mortality exceeding 2% of the flock — paramyxovirus and canker are the most common causes of elevated losses.

Pigeons thrive in hot, dry conditions (35-45°C) with minimal water. In the Middle East and North Africa, traditional dovecotes (burj al-hamam) house 500-2,000 pairs with zero supplemental feed — birds forage entirely on wild seeds and agricultural waste within a 5 km radius.

Pigeons tolerate cold well (surviving to -20°C in insulated lofts) but need protection from wind and moisture. In northern Europe and Canada, lofts must be insulated (R-10 to R-15 walls) and heated to maintain temperatures above 0°C in winter.

Pigeons are uniquely suited to urban environments — they nest on building ledges, forage on waste grain and food scraps, and require minimal land area. A rooftop loft measuring 4 × 3 m can house 30-50 breeding pairs producing 240-700 squab per year in a space that no other livestock could utilize.

A productive King pigeon pair produces 10-14 squab per year (5-7 clutches × 2 squab). Each squab reaches 450-550 g dressed weight at 26-30 days — annual meat per pair: 4.5-7.7 kg dressed. A loft of 20 pairs produces 200-280 squab per year (90-154 kg dressed meat) while consuming 584 kg of grain ($234-350). At $8-15/kg, annual squab revenue: $720-2,310. Net margin: $282-1,875 per loft — one of the highest revenue-per-square-meter ratios of any livestock enterprise.

(naturally mating, slow growth): Heritage turkeys maintain the ability to breed naturally, forage actively, and live normal lifespans. They grow to market weight in 24-30 weeks, yielding a more flavorful but leaner carcass than commercial types.

Metallic bronze and steel-grey plumage. Calm temperament, good foragers. Toms 13-15 kg, hens 6-8 kg. Cold-hardy and disease-resistant. Excellent range bird. One of the oldest heritage varieties, descended from wild turkeys crossed with domesticated European stock.
Coppery-bronze plumage with white-edged tail feathers. Toms 13-16 kg, hens 7-9 kg. Hardy and productive, good foragers. The foundation breed from which Broad Breasted Bronze was developed.
Chestnut-red body with white tail and flight feathers. Toms 11-13 kg, hens 5-7 kg. Active foragers, good temperament. Well-suited to pasture-based systems.
Smaller breed, white with black-edged feathers. Toms 7-9 kg, hens 4-5 kg. Excellent foragers, attractive appearance. Better suited for pest control and ornamental roles than meat production.
(artificial insemination required): Selected for rapid growth and maximum breast meat yield. Cannot mate naturally due to breast size. Grow to market weight in 14-18 weeks.
Large, coppery-bronze plumage. Toms 15-20 kg at maturity, hens 8-12 kg. Fast-growing, heavy breast yield. Most common commercial variety.
White-feathered commercial standard. Toms 16-22 kg, hens 8-14 kg. White feathers leave clean skin appearance after plucking. Industry standard for supermarket production.

(0-8 weeks): 28-30% protein for rapid early growth. Crumble form preferred over mash for poults. Feed ad libitum. Poults are notoriously slow to start eating and drinking — place feed on shallow trays or cardboard for the first few days so they can see it easily. Add clean marbles or small stones to water dishes to prevent drowning and attract attention to the water. Starter feed consumption: approximately 1-1.5 kg per poult over 8 weeks.

(8-16 weeks): 20-24% protein. Transition gradually over 5-7 days by mixing starter and grower. Pellets or crumbles. Free-choice feeding for maximum growth, or controlled feeding (2x daily measured portions) for heritage breeds to prevent overly rapid skeletal development. Feed conversion ratio: approximately 2.5-3.0 kg feed per kg gain for heritage breeds, 2.0-2.5 for commercial types.
(16+ weeks): 16-18% protein with increased energy (added grain). For heritage birds finishing on pasture, supplement with 50-100 g grain per bird per day to improve finish and fat cover.

(0-6 weeks): Poults are more fragile than chicks during the first 2 weeks. Brooding temperature: start at 35-38°C, reduce by 3°C per week until ambient temperature reached. Critical: poults must learn to eat and drink quickly. Dip each poult's beak in water upon placement to teach drinking. Place feed on visible flat surfaces. Keep brooder draft-free but well-ventilated. Mortality can reach 10-20% in first 2 weeks if management is poor — good brooding practices reduce this to under 5%. Guard ...

(*Histomonas meleagridis*): The most critical disease concern for turkeys. Transmitted by cecal worm (*Heterakis gallinarum*) eggs ingested from contaminated soil or earthworms. Symptoms: sulfur-yellow droppings, lethargy, darkened skin of head (cyanosis), weight loss. Mortality: 70-100% in turkeys. Prevention: strict separation from chickens, avoid ranging on land used by chickens within the past 3 years. No reliable treatment available in many regions — prevention is the only strategy.

Turkey eggs (70-80 g, speckled brown or cream) should be collected at least twice daily and stored pointed-end-down at 12-15°C with 75-80% relative humidity for up to 7-10 days before setting in the incubator. Turn stored eggs 90° twice daily to prevent yolk adhesion. Incubator settings: 37.5°C, 55-60% humidity for days 1-25, turning 3-5 times daily. Increase to 65-70% humidity for days 26-28 (lockdown). Hatch rate from fertile eggs: 70-85% with proper incubation. Cool eggs for 5-10 minutes d...

Heritage turkey hens make excellent mothers when allowed to go broody. A broody hen sits on 8-12 eggs for 28 days, hatching 6-10 poults with attentive care for the first 8-10 weeks. Natural brooding eliminates incubator equipment costs and produces calmer, more capable poults that learn foraging from their mother. However, natural brooding limits production to the spring season and the number of broody hens available. Artificial incubation enables year-round production and larger batch sizes ...

Maintain a breeding ratio of 1 tom per 8-10 hens for heritage breeds. Toms become territorial during breeding season — house breeding groups separately to prevent fighting. Select breeding stock based on: conformation (broad breast, straight back, sound legs), growth rate (select fastest-growing 20% of toms and largest-framed 20% of hens), and disease history (never breed from birds that have survived blackhead or respiratory disease). Heritage turkeys maintain fertility for 3-5 years, with p...

Turkeys are surprisingly cold-hardy once mature — heritage breeds tolerate temperatures to -20°C with dry, draft-free shelter and adequate feed. Increase feed by 15-20% during sustained cold (below -10°C) as metabolic rate rises to maintain body temperature.

Turkeys are susceptible to heat stress above 35°C, exhibiting panting, wing-drooping, and reduced feed intake. Provide shade structures (3-4 m² per 10 birds) with misters or wet sand for evaporative cooling. Ensure water availability increases to 1.0-1.5 L per bird per day above 30°C.

Turkeys excel on range systems with mixed pasture and woodland, where they forage for grasshoppers (consuming 100-200 per bird per day during peak insect season), weed seeds, berries, and acorns. Stocking rate: 20-25 m² per bird on good range.

Slaughter at 14-30 weeks depending on breed type. Scald at 60-65°C for 30-60 seconds (longer than chickens due to heavier feathering). Large toms may require two people for safe handling during processing.

Unlike ducks and geese, turkeys are relatively lean birds with only 3-7% body fat. However, the carcass bones make excellent stock — simmer a turkey frame in 6-8 L water with onions, celery, and carrots for 3-4 hours to produce 4-5 L of rich stock with 2-3% protein content.

Turkey feathers have been valued for centuries. Wing feathers (primaries and secondaries) are used for fletching arrows, quill pens, and ceremonial decorations. A mature turkey yields 150-250 g of feathers, with the large tail feathers (12-18 per bird, 30-45 cm long) being the most valuable.

Smoked turkey breast commands $15-25 per kg at retail, compared to $5-8 per kg for fresh whole turkey. Smoke at 80-100°C for 4-6 hours using hardwood (hickory, apple, or cherry) to an internal temperature of 74°C.

Weigh a sample of 15-20 birds weekly from hatch to processing. Heritage breeds should follow a growth curve reaching 200-300 g/week gain during weeks 8-16. Commercial breeds gain 350-500 g/week during the same period.

Track total feed consumed per batch against total dressed meat produced. Target FCR: 2.5-3.0 for heritage breeds, 2.0-2.5 for commercial types. Feed represents 65-75% of total production cost, making FCR the most important economic metric.

Record all deaths with age, date, and observed symptoms. Poult mortality (0-2 weeks) should be under 5% with good management. Grower mortality (2-16 weeks) should be under 3%. Investigate any weekly mortality exceeding 1%.

Inspect 10-20 birds weekly for signs of illness: drooping wings, ruffled feathers, nasal discharge, swollen sinuses, or abnormal droppings. Check litter condition — wet caked litter indicates ventilation or water system problems.

Turkey poults require the highest protein content of any domestic poultry — 28-30% crude protein for the first 8 weeks, declining to 20-24% during weeks 8-16, and 16-18% for finishing. Adult breeder hens require 14-16% protein with 2.5-3.0% calcium during the laying season.

Turkeys require higher levels of several nutrients compared to chickens: methionine (0.50-0.55% of diet vs 0.38-0.45% for chickens), lysine (1.40-1.55% vs 1.00-1.20%), and niacin (70-90 mg/kg feed vs 30-35 mg/kg). Niacin deficiency causes perosis (slipped tendon) in poults within 2-3 weeks.

On good range with mixed pasture and woodland, turkeys obtain 20-40% of their dietary intake from forage during spring through autumn. This reduces feed costs proportionally — a turkey on good range might consume $8-12 in purchased feed versus $12-18 for a fully confined bird to reach market weight.

Heritage turkey breeds reach 6-12 kg live weight at 24-30 weeks on pasture with a feed conversion ratio of 2.5-3.0 kg feed per kg gain. Commercial broad-breasted types reach 8-18 kg at 14-20 weeks with FCR of 2.0-2.5. Toms grow 30-40% faster and heavier than hens. Dressed yield: 75-80% of live weight — the highest dressing percentage of any common poultry. Breast meat constitutes 25-35% of live weight in commercial types. Heritage hens lay 80-120 eggs per year at 70-80 g each, concentrated in...

A heritage tom reaching 10 kg live weight at 28 weeks consumes 25-30 kg of feed ($10-18) and yields 7.5-8.0 kg dressed carcass ($60-120 retail). Net margin per bird: $42-102. A small flock of 20 heritage turkeys on 400 m² of range produces 100-160 kg of dressed meat valued at $800-2,400 with feed costs of $200-360. Heritage breeds breed naturally, eliminating the need for artificial insemination equipment — the key advantage for bootstrapping.

(*Gallus gallus domesticus*): The universal poultry species. Chickens are productive, adaptable, and easy to manage. Dual-purpose breeds provide both meat (1.5-4.5 kg at 12-16 weeks) and eggs (200-300 per year). They scratch and forage, controlling insects and weeds in orchards and gardens. Manure is nitrogen-rich (1.5% N). The foundation species for any poultry operation — start here.

(*Coturnix coturnix japonica*): The smallest poultry species but among the most prolific. Quail begin laying at 6-7 weeks, producing 250-300 tiny eggs (10-12 g each) per year. Extremely space-efficient — can be raised in stacked cages or small aviaries. Fast generation turnover (egg to egg in 8-10 weeks) enables rapid flock expansion. Best suited for egg production in space-constrained settlements.

(*Anas platyrhynchos domesticus*): Hardy, disease-resistant, and excellent foragers in wet environments. Ducks produce rich eggs (70-80 g, higher fat content than chicken eggs) and premium meat. They thrive in marshy or riparian areas where chickens struggle. Excellent pest control in rice paddies and irrigated fields. Khaki Campbell and Pekin are the dominant egg and meat breeds respectively.

(*Anser anser domesticus*): The largest poultry species, geese are primarily grazing birds that convert grass directly to meat and fat with minimal grain supplementation. Goose fat is a premium cooking fat. Geese are territorial and aggressive — effective as guard animals and weeders in specialty crops (cotton, strawberry, orchard). Seasonal layers (30-60 eggs/year) but long-lived (15-25 years).

(*Meleagris gallopavo*): The largest poultry species raised primarily for meat. Heritage breeds (8-15 kg toms) grow slowly but breed naturally; commercial broad-breasted types reach 15-20 kg but require artificial insemination. Must be separated from chickens due to blackhead disease susceptibility. Require more space and different housing than chickens but yield a premium carcass with distinctive flavor.

(*Numida meleagris*): Hardy African poultry specializing in pest control. A flock of 20-30 birds reduces tick populations by 70-90% on 1-2 hectares. Loud alarm calls serve as guardian warnings for all livestock. Extremely disease-resistant. Produce modest amounts of flavorful meat (1.2-1.6 kg) and small speckled eggs (35-40 g). Free-range specialists that forage 60-80% of their diet. Keets are fragile for the first 2 weeks.

(*Columba livia*): Self-foraging birds that produce premium squab meat (350-500 g at 26-30 days) with minimal feed input. Pigeon guano is the richest common animal manure (4-5% N, 2-3% P, 1.5-2% K) — worth more as fertilizer than any other poultry product per kilogram. Both parents feed squab via crop milk, enabling rapid growth without external feed inputs. Homing ability enables messenger services over long distances. Minimal infrastructure — a simple loft suffices.
Secure, enclosed structures with wire mesh (1-2 cm openings) on all vents and openings. Solid doors that close and latch at night.
Perimeter fencing (wire mesh or electric) around range areas. Electric fence at 10-15 cm and 30-40 cm above ground deters foxes, raccoons, and dogs.
Hawks and owls are significant daytime and nighttime predators respectively. Covered runs or netting over range areas reduce aerial predation.
Most ground predators hunt at night. Train birds to return to housing at dusk and close doors securely.
Guinea fowl alarm calls alert all poultry to danger. Geese are aggressive and territorial, deterring small predators. Livestock guardian dogs protect entire range areas.
Corn, wheat, oats, barley, sorghum (milo). Corn is highest energy; oats and barley are lower energy but higher fiber.
Soybean meal, peas, fish meal, meat scraps, insects. Growing birds need 20-30% protein; adult layers need 14-18%.
Oyster shell or limestone grit, free-choice for layers. Essential for eggshell formation.
Small stones for gizzard grinding, especially for whole-grain diets.
Greens (fresh forage), sprouted grains, or supplemental premix. Free-range birds obtain most vitamins from forage; confined birds need supplementation.
A broody hen (chicken, duck, goose) incubates eggs and raises young. Lowest cost, lowest labor, but limited to the hen's capacity (8-15 eggs depending on species). Not all breeds go broody reliably.
Temperature 37.5°C, humidity 55-65%, automatic turning. Enables large-scale production independent of broody behavior. Requires reliable heat source and monitoring.
Chicken hens can incubate eggs of smaller species (quail, guinea fowl, some duck eggs). Useful when the target species has poor broody instinct.

All poultry can carry *Salmonella* and *Campylobacter*. Wash hands after handling birds, eggs, or litter. Cook poultry meat and eggs thoroughly. Pregnant women should avoid cleaning poultry litter (listeria risk from contaminated dust).

Poultry dust (feather dander, dried droppings, bedding particles) causes respiratory irritation and allergic reactions. Wear a mask when cleaning enclosed poultry housing. Ensure good ventilation in all housing.

Wild waterfowl are natural reservoirs. Prevent contact between domestic poultry and wild birds. Report unusual mortality events immediately. High-pathogenicity strains are dangerous to both birds and humans.

A basic poultry house for 50 layers requires 5-10 m² of indoor floor space (0.1-0.2 m² per bird) plus 200-300 m² of outdoor run (4-6 m² per bird). Construction: timber frame (75 × 100 mm posts), solid walls (tongue-and-groove boards or plywood), corrugated metal or shingle roof with 20-30° pitch. Floor: concrete or compacted earth with 10-15 cm deep litter. Ventilation: 0.1 m² of opening per 10 birds at the roofline, covered with 2.5 cm hardware cloth. Poultry feed stored in rodent-proof metal bins (35-50 L capacity each) at below 15% moisture prevents mold and pest contamination. A flock of 50 layers consuming 5-7.5 kg of feed daily requires 150-225 kg of monthly storage. Three to four metal garbage cans with tight-fitting lids suffice. A single rat consumes 20-30 g of feed daily and contaminates 10× that amount — rodent control saves 5-10% of total feed costs annually.

Nipple drinkers (6-8 birds per nipple) or bell drinkers (1 per 50 birds) provide clean water without spillage. A 50-bird flock requires 12-20 L of water daily (250-400 mL per bird), doubling in hot weather. Gravity-fed systems from an elevated reservoir (100-200 L tank on a 1.5-2.0 m platform) supply multiple drinker lines without pumps. In freezing climates, heated water bowls (150-250 watt) or twice-daily manual filling prevents ice formation. Water consumption drops of 10-20% reduce egg pr...

A flock of 50 hybrid layers produces 40-45 eggs per day at peak (80-90% lay rate) from 22-72 weeks of age, declining 10-15% per year thereafter. Annual egg output per hen: 250-300 eggs (15-18 kg of egg mass). Feed conversion: 2.0-2.5 kg feed per kg of egg mass. Each egg contains approximately 6 g protein, 5 g fat, and 70 kcal. At a feed cost of $0.40-0.60 per kg, each egg costs $0.05-0.08 in feed to produce. Annual revenue from 50 layers: 12,500-15,000 eggs, retailing at $0.20-0.50 each ($2,5...

Broilers reach 2.0-2.5 kg at 6-8 weeks with a feed conversion ratio of 1.5-1.8 kg feed per kg of live weight — the most efficient of any terrestrial livestock. Dressed yield: 70-75% of live weight. A batch of 50 broilers consumes 150-225 kg of feed over 7 weeks at a feed cost of $60-135. Heritage breeds grow to 2.0-2.5 kg in 12-16 weeks on range with a feed conversion of 2.5-3.5 but require no medicated feed and reproduce naturally.

A flock of 50 layers produces 5-7.5 kg of manure daily (approximately 1.8-2.7 tonnes per year). Composted poultry manure (1.5% N, 1.0% P, 0.5% K) applied at 2-5 kg per m² fertilizes 360-1,350 m² of garden beds annually — enough to sustain a substantial vegetable garden. Nitrogen value alone: 27-40 kg of N per year, equivalent to 130-190 kg of ammonium sulfate fertilizer ($40-60 value).

Fresh eggs stored at 4°C maintain grade A quality for 4-6 weeks. Waterglass (sodium silicate solution, 1 part sodium silicate to 10 parts water) preserves eggs for 6-12 months at 10-15°C by sealing shell pores — submerge clean, unwashed eggs completely in the solution in a stone crock or food-grade plastic container. Mineral oil coating (dipping each egg in food-grade mineral oil, air-drying, storing at 10-15°C point-down) extends shelf life to 4-6 months. Salt curing (packing eggs in coarse ...

Poultry meat preserved by salting (dry salt rub of 3-4% body weight, refrigerated 5-7 days), smoking (hot smoke at 60-80°C for 2-4 hours or cold smoke at 20-30°C for 12-24 hours over hardwood), or drying (jerky: sliced breast meat salted at 2-3% and dried at 55-60°C for 6-12 hours to below 20% moisture) extends shelf life from days to months. Smoked poultry keeps 2-4 weeks at 10-15°C; poultry jerky keeps 3-6 months at room temperature in sealed containers. Rendered poultry fat (duck, goose) p...

Chicken feathers (80-120 g per bird at processing) are 90% keratin protein by weight. Industrial feather meal (autoclaved at 140°C for 30-60 minutes, then ground) provides a slow-release nitrogen fertilizer (12-14% N) releasing over 4-6 months. Down and small feathers from ducks and geese fill pillows (500-800 g per pillow), quilts (800-1200 g per duvet), and insulated clothing. Primary flight feathers from geese (25-35 cm length) serve as quill pens — cut at a 45° angle and slit to create a ...

terms.definition: Chicks require 20-24% crude protein in starter feed (0-6 weeks), decreasing to 16-18% in grower (6-12 weeks) and 14-16% in layer ration. Ducklings need 18-22% starter protein; goslings 18-20%; turkey poults the highest at 28-30%. Quail chicks require the highest sustained protein at 24-28% for the first 3 weeks. Protein sources in order of biological value: fish meal (72-78% protein, excellent amino acid profile), soybean meal (44-48% protein, widely available), peas (22-26% protein), and ins...

Laying hens require 3.5-4.0% calcium in their diet (compared to 0.9-1.0% for non-layers) — each egg shell contains approximately 2.0-2.5 g of calcium carbonate deposited over 18-20 hours during shell formation. Free-choice oyster shell or limestone grit (2-5 mm particle size) allows hens to self-regulate calcium intake. Phosphorus requirement: 0.3-0.4% available phosphorus in the diet, provided by grain (0.25-0.35% P) and supplemented by bone meal or dicalcium phosphate if needed. Calcium-to-...

Metabolizable energy needs range from 11.5-13.5 MJ/kg of feed for most poultry species. Corn provides the highest energy density (13.5-14.0 MJ/kg), followed by wheat (12.5-13.5 MJ/kg), oats (10.5-11.5 MJ/kg), and barley (10.0-11.0 MJ/kg). Fats and oils (vegetable oil, animal tallow) added at 1-3% of diet increase energy density and improve feed palatability — each 1% added fat increases dietary energy by approximately 0.35 MJ/kg.

Weekly: observe flock for signs of illness (lethargy, ruffled feathers, abnormal droppings, reduced feed/water intake). Monthly: clean and disinfect waterers and feeders; check for external parasites (mite and lice examination at the vent area). Quarterly: complete coop cleanout, fresh bedding, and lime wash on walls. Annually: replace 20-25% of the laying flock with young pullets to maintain peak production. Vaccination schedule (where applicable): Marek's disease (day 1, subcutaneous), Newc...

Footwear disinfection (walk-through boot bath with 2% sodium hydroxide or commercial disinfectant) at every poultry area entrance. Dedicated tools (rake, shovel, feed scoop) for each species area — never shared between turkey and chicken zones. Quarantine all new birds for 30 days in a separate building at least 15 m from the main flock. Rodent control: maintain bait stations or traps at the perimeter of all poultry housing; rodent populations above 5-10 per building significantly increase di...

Candle eggs by holding each against a bright light source (LED flashlight, 100+ lumens) in a darkened room. Fresh eggs show a tight, centered yolk with minimal air cell (under 3 mm depth). Stale eggs have a large, mobile yolk and air cell above 5 mm. Blood spots (ruptured blood vessel during ovulation, visible as a red dot in the yolk) occur in 1-2% of eggs and are safe to eat — not a sign of fertilization. Meat spots (brown tissue fragments in the white) occur in less than 1% of eggs and are...

4-5.5 kg mature weight. White coat (albino). The industry standard meat breed. Rapid growth: kits reach 2 kg live weight at 8 weeks. Calm temperament. Excellent mothers (good nest-building, high milk production, rarely cannibalize kits). Dressing percentage: 55-60%. Most widely available breed.

3.5-5 kg. White body with dark points (nose, ears, feet, tail). Second most popular meat breed. Slightly smaller than New Zealand White but similar growth rate. Often crossed with New Zealand White for hybrid vigor (crossbred kits grow 10-15% faster than purebreds).

3.5-4.5 kg. Short, plush, velvety fur (guard hairs same length as undercoat). Dual-purpose: meat and pelt. Rex pelts are the most commercially valuable rabbit pelts — the dense, uniform fur is used for garment trim, hats, and toys. Growth rate slightly slower than New Zealand White.

2.5-3.5 kg. Entire body covered in long, silky fiber including face and ears. Finest Angora fiber (12-14 microns). Requires daily grooming to prevent matting. Yield: 400-500 g/year per rabbit. Most labor-intensive Angora breed.

3.5-4.5 kg. Long fiber on body, clean face and ears. Coarser than English (14-16 microns) but easier to maintain. Yield: 500-800 g/year. Guard hairs provide structure to the yarn. Most popular Angora breed for hand-spinners.
4.5-6+ kg. Largest Angora breed. High yield: 800-1200 g/year. Fiber diameter 14-16 microns. Requires less frequent grooming (fiber is less prone to matting). The workhorse of Angora production.

5-7 kg (up to 10 kg). Largest rabbit breed. Slow growth rate — not economical for meat alone. Useful as a terminal sire (breed Flemish Giant buck to New Zealand White does for larger fryers). Docile temperament.
4-5 kg. Black or blue coat with silver-tipped guard hairs. Dual-purpose meat and pelt. Hardy and good mothers. Rare breed.

(unlimited): Timothy, orchard grass, brome, or mixed grass hay. The foundation of the diet — provides fiber essential for gut health and dental wear. Feed free-choice (always available). Avoid alfalfa hay for adult rabbits (too high in calcium and protein — causes urinary stones and obesity).

(measured): Commercial rabbit pellets are 16-18% protein, 2-4% fat, 14-20% fiber. Feed 100-150 g/day per adult rabbit (adjust for size and production status). Pregnant and nursing does receive unlimited pellets. Growing fryers receive unlimited pellets until 12 weeks, then restrict to prevent obesity.

(supplement): Grass, clover, dandelion leaves, plantain, vegetable trimmings. Introduce gradually to prevent digestive upset. Never feed iceberg lettuce (too much water, causes diarrhea). Avoid potatoes, rhubarb, and chocolate (toxic).
50-100 mL per kg body weight per day (100-300 mL for a typical adult). Nursing does drink 2-4× normal amounts. Use nipple waterers or crocks. Must be clean and available at all times.

12-24 hours after kindling: remove any dead kits (doe will not cannibalize healthy kits if well-fed, but dead kits attract flies and cause disease). Count live kits. If more than 8-10, consider fostering extras to a doe with a smaller litter (rub the fostered kit with the foster doe's fur to transfer scent).
Return the doe to the buck 2-4 weeks after kindling (or at weaning). Some producers "race breed" (rebreed 1-2 weeks post-kindling) for maximum output, but this taxes the doe.

terms.term: Annual production from a single doe

terms.definition: Harvest loose, mature fiber by gently pulling it from the rabbit's coat. The rabbit naturally releases mature fiber — pulling does not hurt when done correctly. Plucked fiber is longest and cleanest (4-8 cm staple length). Harvest every 90-100 days (3-4 times per year). Labor-intensive but produces the highest quality fiber. Most Angora producers use this method.

Cut fiber with scissors or electric clippers. Faster than plucking but produces shorter, more variable fiber length and includes more guard hairs. Shear every 90 days. Less stress on the rabbit if done skillfully.
Use a fine-toothed comb to remove loose fiber. Intermediate between plucking and shearing. Useful for maintenance grooming between full harvests.

(gastric stasis): Angoras ingest loose fiber during grooming. Unlike cats, rabbits cannot vomit. Fiber accumulates in the stomach, forming a blockage that prevents food passage. Symptoms: reduced appetite, small or no droppings, hunched posture. Prevention: daily grooming to remove loose fiber, unlimited grass hay (fiber keeps the gut moving), weekly papaya or pineapple enzyme treatment (bromelain/papain may help break down wool in the stomach). Wool block is the leading cause of death in Ang...
(fresh weight basis): - Nitrogen (N): 2.0-2.4% - Phosphorus (P₂O₅): 1.0-1.4% - Potassium (K₂O): 0.5-1.0% - Calcium: 1.0-1.5%
severe form producing thick, gelatinous mucus in the droppings. Often fatal in 1-2 days. Triggered by stress and dietary disruption.
(with 1 buck): approximately 10-15 m² of cage space, plus 5-10 m² for feed storage, processing area, and aisles. Total: 15-25 m².

when lifting — one hand under the chest, the other supporting the rump. Never pick up by the ears or scruff alone.

("rabbit fever"): bacterial disease (*Francisella tularensis*) transmitted by ticks and direct contact with infected rabbits. Wear gloves when processing rabbits. Cooking kills the bacteria. Symptoms in humans: fever, swollen lymph nodes, skin ulcer at infection site.
fungal skin infection transmitted by contact. More common in Angora rabbits (dense fur retains moisture). Wear gloves when handling affected animals.
24-26°C, 75-80% relative humidity. Young larvae are sensitive to cold and drying.
22-24°C, 65-75% humidity. Slightly cooler and drier conditions prevent disease in the dense final-stage colonies.

Bamboo or wooden trays, typically 90 x 60 cm, with 2-5 cm raised edges. Each tray holds 200-500 larvae depending on instar. Stack trays on wooden or bamboo racks, spaced 15-20 cm apart vertically for air circulation and access. A rack holding 20 trays at 5 levels supports 4,000-10,000 larvae per rearing cycle.

Remove frass, shed skins, and dead or diseased larvae daily. Transfer larvae to a clean tray by placing fresh leaves on top of the colony and letting the larvae crawl onto them, then moving the leaves to the clean tray. Handle larvae as little as possible. Physical injury causes infection.

When 5th instar larvae stop feeding and begin wandering, transfer them to spinning mounts. Traditional mounts are straw bundles, corrugated cardboard frames, or paper cones arranged on trays. Each larva needs a separate cell or space roughly 3 x 3 cm. Spinning density: 400-500 cocoons per m² of mount surface.

(*Nosema bombycis*): Microsporidian parasite transmitted through eggs or feces. Causes irregular growth, molting failure, and death. No cure. Prevention: screen breeding stock microscopically and destroy infected eggs. This disease collapsed the French silk industry in the 1860s before Louis Pasteur developed screening methods.

Bacterial gut infection causing lethargy, diarrhea, and death. Triggered by overheating, high humidity, or contaminated feed. Remove affected larvae immediately. Reduce humidity and improve ventilation.
(nuclear polyhedrosis): Viral infection causing larvae to become swollen, glossy, and lethargic. Spreads through frass and body fluids. No treatment. Destroy infected larvae and disinfect trays.

(fungal): White or green fungus growing on and mummifying larvae. Caused by excessive humidity. Remove infected individuals. Reduce moisture. Disinfect trays with 2% formaldehyde solution or slaked lime wash between rearing cycles.
Spread cocoons in thin layers on mats in direct sun for 2-3 days. Ambient temperature must reach 40-50°C for effective kill. Simple but weather-dependent and slow.
Expose cocoons to steam at 100°C for 5-10 minutes. Kills pupae quickly and uniformly. Requires a steaming rack over a boiling pot. Most common traditional method in established silk regions.
Dry cocoons in a heated chamber at 60-70°C for 6-8 hours. Even heating, good for large batches. Requires a purpose-built oven or drying room.

A hand-turned reel consisting of a wheel 0.5-1.0 m in diameter, a traversing guide that spreads the thread evenly across the reel width, and a cocoon basin (pot of hot water where cocoons float as their filaments are drawn off). Reeling speed: 100-200 m/min. One skilled worker reels 500-800 g of raw silk per day, processing roughly 2,000-3,000 cocoons.
Silk fabric gloves prevent static discharge and particulate contamination. Used in clean environments.

Thin silk paper, layers of flattened silk thread bonded with shellac or varnish, insulates transformer windings and motor coils. Silk paper has higher dielectric strength than cotton and can be made thinner. This application persists in some high-voltage equipment.
Recovered from degumming liquor by precipitation with alcohol or acid. Used as an adhesive, coating, and cosmetic ingredient.

Cocoon floss, dust, and frass become airborne during sorting and stifling. Prolonged inhalation causes respiratory irritation and allergic reactions. Work in ventilated spaces. Wear a cloth mask over nose and mouth when handling large quantities of dry cocoons.

The reeling basin holds water at 95-100°C. Hands and forearms pass near the surface repeatedly. Burns from splashing or accidental immersion are the most common reeling injury. Use long tongs or bamboo sticks to handle cocoons in the basin. Keep a bucket of cool water nearby for immediate first aid.

High humidity (70-80%) maintained over weeks creates ideal mold conditions on trays, walls, and floors. Aspergillus and other molds cause respiratory disease. Clean and disinfect the rearing room between cycles. Replace moldy trays. Ensure ventilation actually exchanges air, not just circulating it.
Steam at 100°C causes scalds faster than hot water. Use tongs or thick gloves when loading and unloading steaming racks. Do not lean over the steam source.

Dried cocoons stored for extended periods attract dermestid beetles, which bore through the cocoon wall and consume the pupal remains. Infested cocoons cannot be reeled for quality silk. Store dried cocoons in sealed containers or bags, and inspect regularly for signs of insect damage.

(selected for fleece quality and quantity): - **Merino**: The gold standard for fine wool. Fiber diameter 17-24 microns (ultrafine lines can reach below 15 microns). Fleece weight 4-6 kg (greasy). Dense, crimpy fiber that felts well and produces soft, next-to-skin garments. Merinos require shearing annually — the fleece does not shed naturally. Hardy and adaptable, though somewhat more susceptible to foot rot in wet conditions. Originated in Spain, now found worldwide. The foundation of the f...

The gold standard for fine wool. Fiber diameter 17-24 microns (ultrafine lines can reach below 15 microns). Fleece weight 4-6 kg (greasy). Dense, crimpy fiber that felts well and produces soft, next-to-skin garments. Merinos require shearing annually — the fleece does not shed naturally. Hardy and adaptable, though somewhat more susceptible to foot rot in wet conditions. Originated in Spain, now found worldwide. The foundation of the fine woolen textile industry.

Longwool breed producing a lustrous, silky fleece of 30-38 microns. Fleece weight 5-8 kg. The longer staple length (15-20 cm) makes Romney wool ideal for worsted spinning and rug weaving. Large frame (rams 100-130 kg), calm temperament. Tolerates wet conditions well — developed in the Romney Marsh of Kent, England.

Dual-purpose cross (Merino × Lincoln) producing medium wool (25-32 microns) and a reasonable carcass. Fleece weight 4-6 kg. Widely adaptable. Good entry breed for operations needing both wool and meat.

(selected for growth rate, carcass conformation, and lambing percentage): - **Suffolk**: Large, polled, black-faced breed. Rams 110-160 kg. Fast-growing lambs reach 40-50 kg live weight by 12-16 weeks on good pasture. Lean carcass with excellent conformation. The dominant terminal sire breed in commercial sheep production — Suffolk rams are crossed onto ewes of other breeds to produce fast-growing market lambs. - **Texel**: White-faced, muscular breed from the Netherlands. Exceptional carcass...

Large, polled, black-faced breed. Rams 110-160 kg. Fast-growing lambs reach 40-50 kg live weight by 12-16 weeks on good pasture. Lean carcass with excellent conformation. The dominant terminal sire breed in commercial sheep production — Suffolk rams are crossed onto ewes of other breeds to produce fast-growing market lambs.

White-faced, muscular breed from the Netherlands. Exceptional carcass conformation — a high ratio of lean meat to fat and bone. Rams 90-130 kg. Lambs grow slightly slower than Suffolks but yield more saleable meat per kg of live weight. Hardy and adaptable.

Hair sheep (shed their coat rather than requiring shearing) developed in South Africa for meat production in arid conditions. Excellent maternal traits, high lambing percentage (150-180%). Eliminates the need for shearing labor — a significant advantage in hot climates where wool is a liability.

The highest-producing dairy sheep breed. 400-600 L milk per lactation (180-210 days) at 6-7% butterfat. Large frame (ewes 70-90 kg). Prolific — lambing percentage 200-230%. The foundation of sheep dairy operations worldwide. Requires high-quality nutrition to sustain milk production.
French dairy breed producing 250-350 L per lactation at 7-8% butterfat. The breed used for Roquefort cheese production. Slightly hardier than East Friesian, better adapted to rocky, arid pasture.

(the primary quality determinant): Measured in microns. Under 19 microns: fine (next-to-skin garments). 19-25 microns: medium (sweaters, outerwear). 25-35 microns: coarse (carpets, rugs, blankets). Above 35 microns: very coarse (industrial felts, insulation).

The length of individual wool fibers. 5-8 cm for fine wools, 15-25 cm for longwools. Affects spinning method — short staples are carded and woolen-spun (fluffy, warm yarn); long staples are combed and worsted-spun (smooth, strong yarn).

Visual and tactile assessment — fineness, crimp (wave pattern), luster, color, vegetable matter contamination, and strength (tender wool breaks along the fiber, caused by illness or nutritional stress during growth).

(higher investment, higher survival): Bring ewes into lambing pens (individual pens, 1.5-2.0 m²) just before lambing. Monitor closely. Assist difficult births — if a ewe has been straining for 30-60 minutes without progress, check presentation. Ensure lambs nurse colostrum within 2 hours — the first milk contains antibodies essential for passive immunity. In cold weather, dry lambs immediately and provide supplemental heat (heat lamps or warming boxes). Lambing pens allow bonding and prevent ...

(lower labor, lower survival): Ewes lamb on pasture with minimal intervention. Suitable for hardy breeds in mild climates. Lamb mortality is higher (15-25% vs 5-10% in intensive systems) but labor costs are minimal. Requires good pasture shelter (hedgerows, topography) for weather protection. Predation (foxes, coyotes, eagles) is a greater risk without constant human presence.

(last 4-6 weeks): This is the most critical nutritional period. The developing fetus(es) occupy increasing abdominal space, compressing the rumen and reducing the ewe's voluntary feed intake at exactly the time her energy requirements are rising dramatically. A ewe carrying twins needs 30-40% more energy in late pregnancy than in early pregnancy.

(twin lamb disease): Metabolic disease caused by inadequate energy intake in late pregnancy. The ewe mobilizes body fat to meet energy needs, producing ketone bodies faster than the liver can metabolize them. Symptoms: lethargy, apparent blindness, staggering, sweet-smelling breath (acetone), progressing to recumbency and death within 2-7 days if untreated.

Shearing the wool from the breech area (around the tail, hindquarters, and udder) to keep the area clean. Done 2-4 weeks before lambing so the ewe's hindquarters are free of dags (fecal-contaminated wool) that newborn lambs can mistake for the udder. Also reduces flystrike risk (blowflies laying eggs in soiled wool, with maggots eating into the living tissue). Crutching is a partial shear — only the breech and belly areas — and is quicker and less stressful than a full shearing.
Place a small rubber band between the tail vertebrae. Blood supply is cut off; the tail sloughs in 2-4 weeks. Simple, quick, bloodless when done very young.
A heated blade that cuts and cauterizes simultaneously. Minimal bleeding. Common in commercial operations.
Cut with a sharp blade, then apply antiseptic. Simple but creates an open wound.
(under 12 months): Slaughter at 35-50 kg live weight, producing a 17-25 kg carcass (45-55% dressing percentage). Mild flavor, tender meat. The most valuable product per kg.
(12-24 months): Stronger flavor, slightly less tender. Heavier carcass (25-35 kg). Good value when surplus animals are available.

(over 24 months): Strong, distinctive flavor. Requires slow cooking (stewing, braising) to tenderize. Underutilized in modern markets but an excellent, flavorful product for a bootstrapping scenario where nothing is wasted. Breeding ewes at the end of their productive life (6-8 years) become mutton.

Rams can be aggressive, especially during the breeding season (autumn). A charging ram can knock an adult down and cause serious injury. Signs of aggression: lowering the head, pawing, charging. Never turn your back on a ram. Use a ram handling shield or staff. Some handlers keep a spray bottle of water — a quick spray to the face interrupts a charge.

Both to the shearer and the sheep. Hand shears or mechanical clippers can cut skin. Keep blades sharp and close to the skin — dull blades require more pressure and are more likely to grab and tear. Treat cuts on sheep immediately with antiseptic (iodine-based). Shearers risk back injury from the repetitive lifting and bending — proper technique (using legs, not back) is essential.

Orf (contagious ecthyma — a parapoxvirus causing painful sores on hands), Q fever (Coxiella burnetii — flu-like illness from birthing fluids), and listeriosis (from contaminated silage). Wear gloves when handling sheep with sores, during lambing, and when processing fleece. Wash hands thoroughly.

New animals should be quarantined for 30 days and tested for diseases (foot rot, caseous lymphadenitis, ovine progressive pneumonia, scrapie) before introduction to the flock. A single infected introduction can devastate a naive flock.

The traditional hooked staff serves multiple purposes: catching sheep by the neck or hind leg, opening gates, and providing a walking aid on rough terrain. A 1.5 m staff with a curved hook (30-40 cm diameter) bent from green wood or fashioned from a natural branch crotch. The hook should be smooth to avoid injuring sheep. Essential handling tool that requires no manufacturing infrastructure beyond a knife and a source of heat for bending wood.

Sheep are vulnerable to predation (wolves, coyotes, foxes, feral dogs, eagles). Guardian animals (livestock guardian dogs such as Great Pyrenees, Akbash, or Maremma) bonded to the flock from puppyhood provide 24-hour protection. A single guardian dog protects 50-200 sheep. Donkeys and llamas also serve as guardians — they are naturally aggressive toward canids and will chase, trample, or kick predators that approach the flock.
